Reproach
rē-prōch´
n. and v. (censure or disgrace cast upon a man; and, in Scripture, the shame a believer bears for Christ's sake)
Old French reprochier, from Latin prope, near — to bring a thing back near to a man, to hold it up before his face. A reproach is a charge kept close enough that he cannot look away from it.

Biblical Definition

Reproach is disgrace laid on a man, and Scripture treats it as a currency Christ's people deliberately accept. Moses chose it: “Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt: for he had respect unto the recompence of the reward” (Heb 11:26). The church is summoned to it: “let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb 13:13). Peter turns it into evidence: “If ye be reproached for the name of Christ, happy are ye; for the spirit of glory and of God resteth upon you” (1Pe 4:14). It fell first on Christ: “the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me” (Psa 69:9). And a different reproach is to be avoided: an elder “must have a good report of them which are without; lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil” (1Ti 3:7).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines reproach as censure mingled with contempt or derision; contumelious or opprobrious language; and shame, infamy, disgrace.

expand to see more

REPROACH, v.t. To censure in terms of opprobrium or contempt.

2. To upbraid; to suggest blame for any thing.

3. To treat with scorn or contempt.

REPROACH, n. Censure mingled with contempt or derision; contumelious or opprobrious language towards any person; abusive reflections.

2. Shame; infamy; disgrace.

3. Object of contempt, scorn or derision.

Key Scripture

Heb 11:26 — "Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt: for he had respect unto the recompence of the reward."

Heb 13:13 — "Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach."

1Pe 4:14 — "If ye be reproached for the name of Christ, happy are ye; for the spirit of glory and of God resteth upon you: on their part he is evil spoken of, but on your part he is glorified."

Psa 69:9 — "For the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up; and the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me."

1Ti 3:7 — "Moreover he must have a good report of them which are without; lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil."

Modern Corruption

Every reproach a Christian attracts is claimed as the reproach of Christ, and Scripture keeps two kinds carefully apart.

expand to see more

Hebrews 11:26 makes reproach a thing a man can esteem — weigh, price, count — and Moses is said to have valued it above the treasures of Egypt, which he had actually seen. The verse is an act of accounting, not of stoicism. He had respect unto the recompence of the reward, meaning he looked at what was on the other side, and the reproach came out light. That is the only way reproach is ever borne well: not by pretending it does not hurt but by having something on the scale against it.

First Peter 4:14 promises the spirit of glory to the reproached, and the very next verse closes the loophole: let none of you suffer as a murderer, or as a thief, or as an evildoer, or as a busybody in other men's matters. The last item is the one that catches Christians. A man may attract genuine contempt by rudeness, by meddling, by an ungracious manner that has nothing of Christ in it, and then file the result under persecution. Peter names that exact case and excludes it from the blessing.

First Timothy 3:7 shows the other direction and is routinely ignored by people who quote the first. An overseer must have a good report of them which are without — a decent reputation among unbelievers — lest he fall into reproach. So the church is not indifferent to what outsiders think; it cares about it enough to make it a qualification for office. The distinction is between the reproach that attaches to Christ's name and the reproach a man earns for himself, and the difference is usually obvious to everyone except him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew cherpah (H2781), reproach, disgrace; charaph (H2778), to reproach, taunt; Greek oneidismos (G3680), reproach; oneidizo (G3679), to revile, upbraid.

expand to see more

Hebrew cherpah (H2781) — reproach, shame; Psalm 69:7–9, 69:19–20, Joshua 5:9, Nehemiah 1:3.

Greek oneidismos (G3680) — reproach; Hebrews 11:26, 13:13, 10:33, Romans 15:3.

Greek oneidizo (G3679) — to reproach, revile; 1 Peter 4:14, Matthew 5:11, Mark 15:32.

Usage

"“Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches” — an act of accounting."

"“Bearing his reproach” — and it is without the camp."

"“A good report of them which are without” — the other half, made a qualification."
